catalog_quote: The phonological word in MalakMalak is a minimal utterance carrying one primary stress. ... In the one, stress falls on the first syllable and all odd-numbered syllables subsequent to this. In the other case stress falls on the second syllable and all even-numbered syllables subsequent to this. ... Word stress carries little functional load in MalakMalak. ... Words of two syllables are stressed on the first syllable ... Trisyllabic words are usually stressed on the first and third syllables ... However ... primary stress may fall on the second syllable, giving the word an emphatic force ... Tetrasyllabic words are usually stressed on the first and third syllables ... Tetrasyllabic auxiliaries receive primary stress on the second, and secondary stress on the fourth, syllables. ... Pentasyllabic words always take primary stress on the second syllable and secondary stress on the fourth ...…

audit.reasoning: The deciding quotation is verbatim in the held Birk 1976 grammar at the stated section/pages (and duplicated in the held Birk 1975 phonology article); the rule string and the Gordon-2002 correction follow directly from the text. Birk is the only grammar/phonology of MalakMalak in Glottolog and no later phonological or instrumental work was found; Tryon 1974, downloaded now, is silent. The record's internal 'contra' flag (8/20 marked examples fit the formalized rule) reflects Birk's own stated optionality (emphatic 2nd-syllable stress in trisyllables, obligatory peninitial stress in tetrasyllabic auxiliaries and under sandhi) rather than a source problem, so no reclassification is indicated; 'fixed-dominant' with initial as the dominant pattern matches Birk's 'usually' statements.

sources.quote: The phonological word in MalakMalak is a minimal utterance carrying one primary stress. ... Word stress carries little functional load in MalakMalak. Primary stress is usually accompanied by raised pitch. ... The only exceptions to this rule are (1) primary stress falls on the phrase-final syllable of yes/no interrogatives and imperatives (see section 1.7.), and (2) where roots are reduplicated, …
